This document provides a comprehensive overview of vascular pathology, covering venous disorders such as varicose veins and deep vein thrombosis, and lymphatic conditions including lymphangitis and lymphoedema.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Vascular pathology includes diseases of arteries, veins and lymphatics that impair blood flow or drainage. Understanding cause, severity and complications guides urgent and long‑term care.

sections.p: Vascular pathology refers to structural or functional abnormalities of blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries) and lymphatics that lead to obstruction, rupture, inflammation or thrombosis.
b: Diagnosis relies on clinical exam plus imaging (ultrasound, CT/MR angiography) and laboratory markers of inflammation or coagulation.

sections.p: Severity is staged by extent of occlusion, tissue loss and systemic impact. For arterial disease, the Fontaine or Rutherford stages are used; for deep vein thrombosis, proximal vs distal location and presence of embolism guide risk.
b: Stage I–IV for peripheral arterial disease (claudication to gangrene).
Proximal DVT = higher embolic risk than distal.

sections.p: Vascular disease arises from atherosclerosis, thrombosis, infection, trauma or systemic disorders. In low‑resource settings, infections and hemoglobinopathies are common contributors.
b: Atherosclerosis – most common cause of arterial occlusion.
Deep vein thrombosis – stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial injury (Virchow’s triad).
Infectious vasculitis – HIV, TB, syphilis, schistosomiasis.
Sickle cell disease – vaso‑occlusive crises in microvasculature.

sections.p: Patients may have pain, swelling, color change, ulceration or loss of pulse. Venous disease often shows edema, varicosities, or skin changes; arterial disease shows claudication, cold limb, or rest pain.
b: Arterial: intermittent claudication, cool pale skin, diminished pulses.
Venous: swelling, heaviness, varicose veins, stasis dermatitis.
Lymphatic: non‑pitting edema, skin thickening, recurrent cellulitis.

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; when a test is unavailable, rely on bedside assessment and basic imaging.

t.b: Is there flow obstruction or thrombosis? → Shows compressibility, velocity changes; confirms DVT or arterial stenosis.
Is peripheral arterial disease present? → ABI <0.9 indicates significant arterial narrowing.
Is thrombosis likely? → Elevated suggests clot but must be interpreted with clinical probability; normal can rule out DVT in low‑risk patients.
What is the anatomic extent of arterial disease? → Visualises stenosis, aneurysm, dissection; use if ultrasound inconclusive.
Is there inflammation or infection? → Elevated ESR/CRP supports vasculitis or infectious causes.

sections.p: Identify features that signal imminent limb loss or systemic danger.
b: Acute limb ischemia: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paralysis, paresthesia, poikilothermia.
Pulmonary embolism from proximal DVT.
Aneurysm rupture or expanding pseudo‑aneurysm.
Severe cellulitis or necrotizing fasciitis in lymphatic obstruction.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, restore flow, prevent recurrence and manage complications.
b: Anticoagulation (heparin → oral vitamin K antagonist or DOAC) for DVT/PE; chosen for rapid effect and monitoring ease.
Antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel) for atherosclerotic disease; avoid in active bleeding.
Statins for atherosclerosis – lower LDL, stabilize plaques.
Compression therapy for chronic venous disease – improves venous return, reduces edema.
Surgical/endovascular revascularisation for critical limb ischemia – bypass or angioplasty.
Antibiotics for infectious vasculitis or cellulitis; cover typical skin flora and regional pathogens (e.g., TB, HIV‑related organisms).

sections.p: Regular monitoring prevents progression and detects early complications.
b: ABI or duplex every 6–12 months for peripheral arterial disease.
Compression stockings and leg elevation for chronic venous insufficiency.
Lifestyle modification: smoking cessation, blood pressure control, diabetes management.
Vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal) to reduce infection‑related vascular events.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic vascular pathology must be distinguished.
b: Peripheral neuropathy – can cause pain and sensory loss without vascular signs.
Musculoskeletal strain – mimics claudication but lacks pulse changes.
Lymphedema vs chronic venous edema – differentiate by pitting nature and skin changes.

sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or false‑positive findings.
b: D‑dimer can be normal in chronic DVT; rely on imaging if suspicion high.
ABI may be falsely normal in calcified arteries (common in diabetes); consider toe‑brachial index.
Compression ultrasound may miss isolated calf DVT; repeat if symptoms persist.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of limb pulse or severe pain (acute limb ischemia).
Shortness of breath with leg swelling (possible pulmonary embolism).
Rapidly expanding leg swelling with fever (possible septic thrombophlebitis).

faq.q: Why is duplex ultrasound the first test for suspected DVT?
faq.a: It is bedside, non‑invasive, shows vein compressibility and flow, and has high sensitivity for proximal DVT.

faq.q: Can a normal ABI rule out peripheral arterial disease?
faq.a: In most patients yes, but in diabetics with calcified vessels a normal ABI may be misleading.

faq.q: When is surgery preferred over anticoagulation for DVT?
faq.a: When there is phlegmasia cerulea dolens, massive clot burden, or contraindication to anticoagulation.

exam: Describe the diagnostic steps and staging for peripheral arterial disease using the ABI and Fontaine classification.
List the three components of Virchow’s triad and give an example of each in a low‑resource setting.
Explain how management differs between acute limb ischemia and chronic peripheral arterial disease.
